El Peñol is included in an excursion route from Medellín to Guatapé. Visitors discover the history of the settlement and explore a replica of the old town with its colonial architecture.

A visit to El Peñol is easy to combine with a trip to the El Peñón de Guatapé rock and a walk through Guatapé. These are separate stops: the town of El Peñol, the monolith, and Guatapé each have their own names and histories. Along the road between the settlements, views open up over the reservoir, green mountains, and indented shorelines.

El Peñón de Guatapé, also known as La Piedra del Peñol, rises above the reservoir in Colombia's Antioquia region. The monolith stands about 220 meters above the surrounding landscape. The rock offers the chance to see the scenery that draws visitors to the area around Guatapé.

At the top, a panorama opens up over the water, green hills, and numerous islands. The intricate shoreline stretches toward the horizon, and from above it is easy to see how the reservoir divides the valleys into separate inlets.

A visit to the rock combines well with a walk through Guatapé. After enjoying the panorama, visitors can admire the colorful facades and decorative reliefs on the lower walls of houses, stroll along the town's streets, and spend time by the water. This day trip from Medellín combines natural scenery with an introduction to local architecture.

El Peral is one of Valparaíso's historic ascensores: small funicular lifts connecting the lower port city with residential neighborhoods on the hills. Its lower station is near the courthouse and Sotomayor Square, while the upper station opens onto Paseo Yugoslavo on Cerro Alegre.

The lift began operating in 1901. Its history is tied to residents' everyday journeys across the city's steep terrain. Today, the short line is interesting both as transport and as part of Valparaíso's architectural heritage.

After the ascent, visitors can continue along Paseo Yugoslavo, overlooking the port. Baburizza Palace is nearby. El Peral, the viewpoint, and the museum in the palace are separate attractions, so their routes and the scope of a visit should be considered individually. Anyone planning to ride the funicular should check its actual operating schedule.

El Porvenir is part of the San Blas island region, which is associated with the Guna people. The small island appears on yacht itineraries along Panama's Caribbean coast. Its shoreline offers a place to disembark and explore the island surroundings from land.

The main impressions are of white beaches and the surrounding waters. A walk on El Porvenir adds a closer encounter with the island to the views from the deck. It is one stop on a journey between other parts of San Blas, where the sea and the lives of local communities shape the experience.
